Patient Information

Vestibular Rehabilitation at Home

Exercises that retrain the balance organ of the inner ear — for dizziness, unsteadiness and the sense that the world moves when you do.

The inner ear does two jobs: it tells your brain which way up you are, and it holds your eyes steady on the world while your head moves. When one side is damaged — by a viral vestibular neuritis, by Ménière's disease, by surgery, or by a cause that is never identified — both jobs fail at once. That is why the room seems to swim when you turn your head, why reading a shelf in a supermarket is unbearable, and why you feel worst in the dark.

The good news is well established: the brain can recalibrate, and the exercises that drive that recalibration are among the best-evidenced treatments in neurology. But they only work if the exercises make you a little dizzy. That is the part patients are rarely told, and the part that decides whether this succeeds.

The rule that governs this whole page

The dizziness is not a side effect of the treatment. It is the treatment. Your brain only learns that its balance signals are wrong when it is given the mismatch to work on. Avoiding movement keeps you dizzy for longer — which is why rest, dark rooms and long-term motion-sickness tablets make people worse.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.
How much symptom is the right amount?
  • Aim to provoke your symptoms to about 3 or 4 out of 10 during an exercise.
  • The symptoms should settle back to your baseline within 15 to 30 minutes of stopping.
  • Feeling somewhat washed out for an hour afterwards, especially in the first two weeks, is normal and expected.
  • If you are still worse the next day, the dose was too high — do fewer repetitions or slower movements, but do not stop altogether.
  • Vomiting, or symptoms that build through the week rather than settling, means it is time to speak to me.
Before you start — making this safe to do alone
  • Always have something solid to grab. A kitchen bench, a heavy table, a wall on each side, or the back of a chair wedged against a wall. Not a wheeled chair, not a towel rail.
  • Choose the right floor. Bare, level, non-slip. Move rugs and cords out of the way. Do not do balance work on a rug edge or a wet bathroom floor.
  • Wear shoes or bare feet, not socks. Well-fitting shoes with a firm heel counter and a thin sole let you feel the floor.
  • If you have fallen in the last six months, or you feel unsafe standing still with your feet together, do not start alone. Do these first with a family member present, or ask me to arrange a physiotherapist.
  • Carry your phone, or wear a personal alarm, if you live alone.
  • Stop and contact your doctor if an exercise causes chest pain, sudden severe dizziness, a new weakness, or a fall.
Where not to do these exercises
  • Never in a car, on stairs, on a ladder, at the stove, or in the bath or shower.
  • Never standing in the middle of a room — a bench, a doorway or a corner, every time.
  • Do not drive during the acute phase of vertigo, and do not drive straight after a session.
  • If you have significant neck disease, previous neck surgery, or known problems with the arteries in your neck, check with me before starting the head-movement exercises.
  • If you have fallen in the past year — especially more than once, or once with an injury — be assessed before doing single-leg, eyes-closed or cushion work on your own.

First — is this actually the right sheet for you?

Vestibular exercises treat some kinds of dizziness and are the wrong treatment for others. Three patterns are worth separating.

🔄 Brief spinning only on moving your head in bed

Intense spinning lasting under a minute, brought on by lying down, rolling over, or looking up — and settling completely in between — is the pattern of BPPV, loose crystals in the inner ear. This is not treated by these exercises. It is cured, usually in one or two visits, by a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley. Tell me, and we will do that instead.

🌊 Constant unsteadiness, worse when you move your head

Persistent imbalance, a sense that the world lags behind your head movements, worse in the dark and on uneven ground, following an episode of severe vertigo weeks or months earlier. This is vestibular hypofunction, and this sheet is written for you.

🛒 Constant dizziness worse in busy visual places

Rocking or swaying present most of the day, worse standing and walking, much worse in supermarkets, traffic, patterned floors and on screens, often after an initial vestibular event that has otherwise recovered. This is persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD). The exercises here help, but graded exposure and, often, medication or psychological therapy matter more — see the last section.

Part 1 — Steadying your vision

The core of vestibular rehabilitation. Little and often beats long sessions: three to five short sessions spread through the day.

Gaze stabilisation — side to side (VOR × 1)

1–2 minutes at a time, 3–5 times a day
Cornerstone of vestibular rehab

Retrains the reflex that keeps your eyes locked on a target while your head moves. When that reflex is damaged, the world appears to bounce or blur when you move — this is the exercise that fixes it.

  1. Sit down. Hold a business card, or a piece of paper with a single large letter on it, at arm's length at eye level. You can also stick it on the wall.
  2. Look at the letter and keep it in sharp focus. Your eyes stay on the target the whole time.
  3. Now turn your head from side to side — a small arc, about 30° each way — while the letter stays perfectly clear.
  4. Go as fast as you can while still keeping the letter in focus. The moment it blurs, you are going too fast: slow down slightly and stay just below that speed.
  5. Continue for 1 minute, then rest until any dizziness settles.
  6. Build up to 2 minutes per session, and do 3 to 5 sessions spread through the day.
Make it harderStand instead of sit. Then stand with feet together. Then do it against a busy background such as a patterned curtain or a bookshelf. Then walk on the spot while doing it.
Make it easierDo 20 seconds at a time and rest. Reduce the speed, not the frequency — little and often is what drives adaptation.
SafetySit down for the first week. If you are unsteady, sit with your back against a chair. Never do this standing at the top of stairs.
Why it worksThe 2022 vestibular hypofunction guideline from the American Physical Therapy Association recommends gaze stabilisation exercises for at least 12 minutes a day in the acute phase and 20 minutes a day for longstanding problems, sustained over 4 to 6 weeks.

Gaze stabilisation — up and down

1–2 minutes, 3–5 times a day
The other half

The same reflex works in the vertical plane, and it is the one you use on stairs, on kerbs, and when looking down at your feet. It is often neglected.

  1. Hold the same target at arm's length at eye level.
  2. Keeping your eyes fixed on it, nod your head up and down through a small arc.
  3. Again, move as fast as you can while the target stays clear.
  4. One minute, then rest. Alternate with the side-to-side version through the day.
Make it harderStanding, then feet together, then against a busy background, then while walking on the spot.
Make it easierSmaller, slower movements, 20 seconds at a time.
SafetyVertical head movement is more likely to provoke nausea. Have a chair, and do it before rather than after meals.
Why it worksAdaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex is direction-specific: training side-to-side movements does not fully transfer to up-and-down movements.

Target-to-target gaze shifts

10 shifts each way, 2–3 times a day
Substitution training

Teaches your eyes and head to work together in a new way, compensating for the part of the reflex that will not recover.

  1. Stick two targets on the wall about a metre apart, at eye level, and sit or stand about a metre away.
  2. Look at the left target with your head facing it.
  3. Move your eyes to the right-hand target first, and only then turn your head to follow, so the eyes lead and the head catches up.
  4. Pause, then reverse the process back to the left.
  5. Do ten each way.
Make it harderMove the targets further apart; do it standing with feet together; add a vertical pair of targets.
Make it easierMove the targets closer together and slow down.
SafetyStop and rest if symptoms climb above the acceptable level described below.
Why it worksSubstitution strategies — using eye movements and neck position sense to fill the gap — are a recognised complement to adaptation exercises in the vestibular hypofunction guideline.

Advanced gaze stabilisation (VOR × 2)

1 minute × 2–3 times a day, once the basic version is easy
Weeks 3–4 onwards

A harder version that demands twice as much from the reflex. Only start it once the basic version is comfortable.

  1. Hold the card at arm's length in front of you.
  2. Move your head and the card in opposite directions at the same time — head left while the card moves right, and vice versa.
  3. Keep the letter in focus throughout.
  4. Start with slow, small movements. One minute at a time is plenty.
Make it harderIncrease speed and range gradually; then perform standing.
Make it easierReturn to the basic version for another week. There is no prize for rushing this.
SafetyThis provokes more symptoms than the basic exercise. Sit down for it initially.
Why it worksVOR × 2 exercises drive a larger adaptation stimulus, but the standard VOR × 1 exercises carry the strongest evidence and remain the foundation.
The dose that has actually been tested

The 2022 clinical practice guideline from the American Physical Therapy Association gives a strong recommendation to offer vestibular rehabilitation for acute, subacute and chronic vestibular hypofunction. Its suggested doses are: gaze stabilisation totalling at least 12 minutes a day in three or more short sessions for recent symptoms; 20 minutes or more a day, in three to five sessions, sustained for four to six weeks, once symptoms are longstanding; and 20–40 minutes a day for five to seven weeks if both ears are affected. Add at least 20 minutes a day of balance and walking work on top of that. Two honest caveats: the decision to treat rests on strong evidence, but the exact numbers are extrapolated from trial protocols rather than tested against each other — so treat them as a target, not a prescription. And you need no equipment: a trial comparing low-tech balance training on a sofa cushion with a virtual-reality system found identical results at eight weeks and six months.

Part 2 — Steadying your body

Retraining balance by systematically taking away the senses you have learnt to rely on.

Standing balance with vision removed

3 × 30 seconds in each position, daily
Forces the inner ear to work

With your eyes open, vision does most of the work and the damaged system stays lazy. Closing your eyes forces the inner ear and the sensation in your feet to take over — which is how they improve.

  1. Stand in a corner, or facing into the corner of a kitchen bench, so support is available on both sides. Have someone nearby the first time.
  2. Stage 1: feet together, eyes open, 30 seconds. Then eyes closed, 30 seconds.
  3. Stage 2: semi-tandem (one heel beside the other big toe), eyes open then closed.
  4. Stage 3: full tandem (heel to toe), eyes open then closed.
  5. Stage 4: repeat the whole sequence standing on a firm sofa cushion or folded pillow, which removes reliable information from your feet as well.
  6. Move to the next stage only when you can hold the current one for 30 seconds without touching down.
Make it harderAdd slow head turns while your eyes are closed — this is demanding and is where most of the remaining gain lives.
Make it easierStay at eyes-open, feet apart, with fingertips resting on the bench.
SafetyNever with your eyes closed in an open room. Corner or bench, every time.
Why it worksBalance training that systematically removes vision and reliable foot sensation is a core recommendation in the vestibular hypofunction guideline, alongside gaze stabilisation.

Walking with head turns

3 lengths of the corridor, most days
Real-world balance

Balance fails when you have to look away from where you are going — checking traffic, reading a shelf, being spoken to. This trains that exact situation safely.

  1. Walk down a clear corridor at your normal pace, within reach of a wall.
  2. As you walk, turn your head slowly to the left, count two steps, then slowly to the right, count two steps. Keep walking in a straight line.
  3. Do one length with side-to-side head turns, then one length nodding up and down.
  4. If you feel dizzy or you veer, stop, steady yourself, and make the head movements slower and smaller.
Make it harderFaster head turns, then adding a task — naming animals, counting backwards from 100 by threes — while you walk.
Make it easierDo the head turns standing still with a hand on the bench before combining them with walking.
SafetyCorridor only. If head turning provokes true spinning vertigo rather than mild unsteadiness, stop and tell me — that is a different problem.
Why it worksHead movement removes visual stabilisation and forces the inner ear and body-position senses to do the work. Dual-task walking training is specifically recommended in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines.

Tandem and semi-tandem standing

3 × 30 seconds each foot in front, daily
Do this with eyes open first, then closed

The static version of tandem walking — the safest way to start if walking heel-to-toe is still too much.

  1. Stand beside a kitchen bench with one hand resting on it.
  2. Put one foot half a step in front of the other, heel beside the opposite big toe (semi-tandem).
  3. Hold for 30 seconds, breathing normally, eyes ahead.
  4. Swap which foot is in front and repeat.
  5. When 30 seconds is comfortable, move the front foot fully in front (true tandem) so heel touches toe.
Make it harderOne fingertip on the bench, then no hands, then eyes closed with a hand hovering over the bench — eyes closed doubles the difficulty and is where the real gains are.
Make it easierFeet together, both hands on the bench, 30 seconds.
SafetyStand facing into the corner of a bench, not out into the room, so there is something to catch on either side.
Why it worksFeet-together, semi-tandem and tandem stance are the standard progression used in the Otago programme and in nearly every trial that reduced falls.

Tandem walking (heel-to-toe), corridor only

10 steps × 3, once a day
Core balance drill

Trains the side-to-side balance control that keeps you upright when you turn, step around something, or are jostled.

  1. Do this in a corridor narrow enough that you can touch both walls with your elbows out, or beside a kitchen bench. Never in the middle of a room.
  2. Stand at one end with your fingertips lightly brushing one wall.
  3. Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel of the front foot touches the toes of the back foot, as if walking a tightrope.
  4. Take ten slow heel-to-toe steps, looking ahead at a point on the wall rather than at your feet.
  5. Turn around carefully — wide, slow steps, not a quick pivot — and walk back.
  6. Rest, then repeat twice more.
Make it harderFingertips off the wall (but still within reach). Then hands folded across your chest. Then walk backwards heel-to-toe. Only when all of that is easy, try it with your head turning slowly side to side.
Make it easierWalk with one whole hand on the wall, and use a semi-tandem step (front heel beside the back toes, not in front of them) until that feels steady.
SafetyNever in an open room, never on a rug, never in socks. If you find yourself repeatedly grabbing the wall, the drill is too hard — go back a stage. Expect this to feel worse than it did before your inner ear was damaged. That is the point of doing it.
Why it worksNarrowing your base of support is the most efficient way to challenge balance, and challenging balance is what makes falls prevention work. In the Cochrane review of 108 trials, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% overall — but programmes that genuinely challenged balance and totalled three or more hours a week reduced falls by around 40%. Comfortable, seated, low-dose programmes did not.

Chair squats (sit-to-stand)

10 repetitions × 2–3 sets, 3 days a week
Highest-value exercise

The single most useful strengthening exercise for an older adult: it is how you get off the toilet, out of the car, and up off the floor after a fall.

  1. Use a firm dining chair with its back against a wall. Not an armchair, not a chair on castors.
  2. Sit forward on the seat with your feet flat, hip-width apart, drawn back slightly so your heels sit under your knees.
  3. Lean your chest forwards over your knees (nose over toes) — this, not leg strength, is what most people are missing.
  4. Push down through your heels and stand up all the way, squeezing your buttocks at the top.
  5. Lower yourself back down slowly — take 3 seconds — and touch the seat lightly rather than dropping onto it.
  6. That is one repetition. Do 10, rest a minute, and repeat.
Make it harderArms folded across the chest instead of pushing off your knees. Then a slower, 4-second lowering. Then a lower seat (a firm cushion removed, or a lower chair). Then stand from the chair and hold a half-squat for 3 seconds before sitting.
Make it easierPush off your thighs or the chair arms with your hands, and use a higher seat with a cushion on it. Even five repetitions counts.
SafetyChair against a wall, every time. If your knees are painful, reduce the depth rather than abandoning the exercise.
Why it worksSit-to-stand is a named component of the Otago programme — which reduced falls by about a third in trials of frail older people with an average age of 81 — and functional balance training of this kind carries a strong recommendation in the 2022 World Guidelines for Falls Prevention.

Part 3 — Turning the sensitivity down

For movement-provoked and visually-provoked symptoms. This is where avoidance is undone.

Habituation — repeating what makes you dizzy

3 repetitions of your 2–3 worst movements, 2 times a day
The dizziness is the treatment

The brain turns down its response to a movement that is repeated often enough and found to be harmless. Avoidance does the opposite: it keeps the alarm turned up.

  1. Identify two or three movements that reliably make you dizzy — for example, lying down and rolling over, looking up at a high shelf, bending to the floor, or turning quickly.
  2. Sitting safely on a bed or firm chair, perform one of them at a moderate speed.
  3. Wait for the dizziness to settle — usually under a minute — then do it again.
  4. Three repetitions, then move on to the next movement.
  5. Do the whole set twice a day. Keep a note of how strong the dizziness is out of 10; over two to four weeks the number should fall.
Make it harderIncrease the speed of the movement, and add movements you have been avoiding in daily life.
Make it easierDo the movement more slowly and in stages, stopping halfway.
SafetyDo this where you cannot fall — sitting on a bed, with the floor clear. If a movement causes intense brief spinning specifically on lying down or rolling over, tell me first: that pattern suggests crystals in the inner ear (BPPV), which is cured by a repositioning manoeuvre, not by exercises.
Why it worksHabituation exercises reduce motion-provoked dizziness and are recommended for people whose main complaint is symptoms brought on by movement.

Getting back into busy places

Once daily, building duration weekly
For visually induced dizziness

For people whose dizziness is worst in supermarkets, on patterned carpets, in traffic or on screens. Avoiding those places makes the sensitivity worse; graded exposure reverses it.

  1. Make a list of visually busy situations, ranked from mildly uncomfortable to worst.
  2. Start with the mildest — perhaps watching a slow-moving video, or standing in a quiet aisle of a shop.
  3. Stay in it until the symptoms begin to settle, or for a set time such as two minutes, rather than leaving at the peak of the discomfort.
  4. Repeat daily until that step is easy, then move up your list.
  5. Do not brace, grip trolleys, or hold your head rigid — stiffening is part of what maintains the problem.
Make it harderLonger exposures, busier places, then adding head movement while you are there.
Make it easierShorter exposure with a companion; start with a photograph or a static pattern.
SafetyChoose places where sitting down is possible. Do not drive somewhere you may not feel able to drive home from.
Why it worksGraded exposure combined with reducing bracing and vigilance is the mainstay of treatment for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD), often alongside medication and, where appropriate, cognitive behavioural therapy.

What to expect, and when

TimeWhat usually happensWhat to do
Days 1–3Symptoms often feel slightly worse. Most people are tired.Halve the repetitions rather than stopping. Keep the daily total up by doing more, shorter goes.
Weeks 1–2The exercises stop being unbearable. Everyday head movements are still unpleasant.Build to the full dose. Start the balance work.
Weeks 3–4Clear improvement in the exercises themselves; daily life beginning to follow.Add the harder progressions — standing, then feet together, then busy backgrounds.
Weeks 6–12Most of the recovery. Residual symptoms are usually situational — supermarkets, driving at night, tiredness.Keep going. Stopping at 80% is the commonest reason people plateau.
Beyond 3 monthsImprovement continues but more slowly.If you have not improved at all by now, come back — the diagnosis may need revisiting.

Things that get in the way of recovery

💊 Motion-sickness tablets

Prochlorperazine (Stemetil), betahistine and similar drugs are useful for a few days during an acute attack of severe vertigo with vomiting. Taken for weeks or months, they suppress the very signals the brain needs in order to recalibrate, and they delay recovery. If you are still taking one, let us plan how to stop it.

🛏️ Rest and avoidance

The instinct to lie still in a dark room is correct for about 48 hours and wrong after that. Every movement you avoid is a movement your brain never gets to recalibrate.

🧊 Holding your head rigid

Most people with dizziness stiffen their neck to keep their head still, and turn their whole body instead. This maintains the problem and adds neck pain to it. Deliberately loosening the neck is part of the treatment — see my neck sheet.

😰 Anxiety and hypervigilance

Anxiety and dizziness feed each other, and monitoring your own balance moment by moment makes it worse — this is the central mechanism in PPPD. Slow breathing and relaxation practice genuinely help here; my stress management page covers the techniques in detail.

🍷 Alcohol

Alcohol directly disturbs the inner ear and interferes with the recalibration. Keep it low while you are doing this programme.

😴 Poor sleep

Dizziness is markedly worse when you are tired, and disturbed sleep is common after a vestibular event. If sleep is the problem, treat it — see my insomnia sheet.

Things people are told that are not true

"Just follow my finger with your eyes — that's the exercise."

This is one of the very few things the guideline actively recommends against, and it does so strongly. Moving the eyes while the head stays still does not generate the error signal the brain needs in order to recalibrate. Across the trials, eye movements without head movement did not work.

The head must move. That is what makes these exercises effective, and it is also why they make you dizzy.

"I should rest until the dizziness settles."

Rest is the single most reliable way to prevent recovery. Beyond the first day or two of an acute attack, every head movement you avoid is a movement the brain never gets to correct. The evidence on this is consistent and it is why this page is written the way it is.

"If the exercise makes me dizzy, I must be doing damage."

No. Provoked dizziness is expected, and it is the mechanism of the treatment — the guideline defines habituation exercises as movements that deliberately cause mild to moderate symptoms. The limit is not whether you feel dizzy but how long it takes to settle: back to baseline within 15 to 30 minutes is right, still worse the next morning means the dose was too high.

"A stronger tablet would help more."

Vestibular suppressants make you feel less dizzy while measurably preventing you from getting better — people taking them daily showed no improvement in their sway measurements over six weeks. In people over 65 they are also associated with roughly a threefold increase in falls. They are for the first day or two of a severe attack with vomiting, and no longer.

"I'm too old for this to work."

Age does not reduce the potential for recovery — that is a strong, high-level statement in the guideline, and older adults should be offered this treatment with the expectation of a good result. What changes with age is that the falls risk while training is higher, which is a reason to be careful about how you do the exercises, not whether.

"I need an app, a headset or special equipment."

You do not. A randomised trial compared low-tech balance training using a foam cushion with a virtual-reality gaming system, and found identical outcomes on every measure at eight weeks and at six months. A kitchen bench, a business card and a sofa cushion are the whole kit.

"I walk and I use the exercise bike, so my balance is being trained."

General fitness training without a balance component has not been shown to reduce vestibular symptoms. It is worth doing for every other reason; it does not substitute for the exercises above.

"The exercises stopped working, so there's nothing more to be done."

Far more often, the exercises stopped changing. If the basic gaze stabilisation has become easy, it has stopped driving any adaptation — that is the signal to make it faster, to do it standing, to do it against a busy background, or to move on to the advanced version. A genuine plateau after proper progression is worth reassessing, and is a reason to come back rather than to give up.

"Holding onto the walls and looking at the floor keeps me safe."

If your legs are genuinely weak, use the aid. But if the problem is dizziness rather than weakness, gripping, stiffening and staring at the ground are exactly what maintain it — this is the central mechanism in persistent postural-perceptual dizziness. The treatment is graded exposure with a deliberately loose neck and eyes up.

Hurt is not the same as harm

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Since 1 July 2025, GP Management Plans and Team Care Arrangements have been replaced by the GP Chronic Condition Management Plan. With one in place, you can access up to five Medicare-rebated allied health services per calendar year — shared across all disciplines, so five physiotherapy sessions means none left for anything else (ten services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients). Referral is now by an ordinary letter rather than a special form. Ask your GP whether you are eligible.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Stop and seek medical attention urgently if you develop
  • Double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial weakness or numbness.
  • New weakness or clumsiness in an arm or leg, or a severe new headache or neck pain.
  • New or fluctuating hearing loss, a feeling of fullness in one ear, or roaring tinnitus with attacks of vertigo lasting twenty minutes to hours.
  • Dizziness that is constant and unremitting from the outset, rather than provoked by movement.
  • Falls, especially falling consistently towards one side.
  • Feeling faint, greying out, or tunnel vision on standing — that is a blood pressure problem, not a balance-organ one, and needs lying and standing blood pressure measured.
  • A first-ever episode of severe vertigo — that needs assessment before you start any exercises.
